home.intro: Every place on Earth has its own address made of two numbers: latitude and longitude. Let's learn how to read it!
explore.keysHint: Tip: use ← and → keys to change steps.

topic.1.step.ball.title: The Earth is a ball
topic.1.step.ball.body: To say exactly where a place is on a ball, we draw an imaginary grid on it. The grid has two kinds of lines: parallels and meridians. Drag the globe to turn it.
topic.1.step.equator.title: The equator
topic.1.step.equator.body: The equator goes around the middle of the Earth. It is the longest parallel and its latitude is 0°. It divides the Earth into the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere.
topic.1.step.parallels.title: Parallels
topic.1.step.parallels.body: Parallels are circles that run parallel to the equator. The closer to a pole, the shorter they are. They tell us the latitude: from 0° at the equator up to 90°N at the North Pole or 90°S at the South Pole.
topic.1.step.angle.title: Why degrees?
topic.1.step.angle.body: Latitude is an angle! Imagine a line from the centre of the Earth to a place. The angle between that line and the equator is the latitude. Drag the point on the circle and watch the angle change.
topic.1.step.meridians.title: Meridians
topic.1.step.meridians.body: Meridians are half-circles that join the North Pole and the South Pole. All meridians are the same length. They tell us the longitude.
topic.1.step.prime.title: The prime meridian and 180°
topic.1.step.prime.body: The prime meridian (0°) goes through Greenwich in London. On the other side of the Earth is the 180° meridian. Together they divide the Earth into the Eastern and Western Hemispheres. Longitude goes from 0° up to 180°E or 180°W.
topic.1.step.projections.title: Many maps, one grid
topic.1.step.projections.body: A flat map is always a little stretched, because the Earth is round. This map is called Equal Earth: every country keeps its true size, so the meridians bend. The coordinates stay the same on every map. Try the Grid map in the Lab to compare.
topic.1.step.tropics.title: Tropics and polar circles
topic.1.step.tropics.body: Some parallels have their own names: the Tropic of Cancer (about 23°N), the Tropic of Capricorn (about 23°S), the Arctic Circle (about 66°N) and the Antarctic Circle (about 66°S).
topic.1.step.play.title: Try it yourself
topic.1.step.play.body: Drag the point around. When is it in the Northern Hemisphere? When is it in the Western Hemisphere? Find the Tropic of Cancer.
topic.2.step.north-south.title: North or south?
topic.2.step.north-south.body: On a map, north is at the top. Warsaw (52°N) is north of the 50°N parallel. Rome (42°N) is south of it. In the Northern Hemisphere a bigger number means further north.
topic.2.step.southern.title: Careful in the south!
topic.2.step.southern.body: In the Southern Hemisphere a bigger number means further south. 40°S is south of 20°S, and 10°S is north of it.
topic.2.step.east-west.title: East or west?
topic.2.step.east-west.body: East is to the right on a map. Kyiv (31°E) is east of the 20°E meridian. London (0°) is west of it. In the Eastern Hemisphere a bigger number means further east.
topic.2.step.western.title: Careful in the west!
topic.2.step.western.body: In the Western Hemisphere a bigger number means further west. 100°W is west of 60°W, and 30°W is east of it.
topic.2.step.across-zero.title: Across the lines
topic.2.step.across-zero.body: Every place with N latitude is north of every place with S latitude. Every place with E longitude is east of Greenwich, and every place with W longitude is west of it.
topic.2.step.play.title: Try it yourself
topic.2.step.play.body: Move the point and say it out loud: is it north or south of the equator? East or west of Greenwich? Then check the coordinates below the map.
topic.3.step.address.title: An address in two numbers
topic.3.step.address.body: Coordinates are written as latitude first, then longitude: 52°N, 21°E. That is Warsaw!
topic.3.step.latitude.title: Step 1: latitude
topic.3.step.latitude.body: Find the parallel that goes through the point and read its number at the left edge of the map. Is the point above the equator (N) or below it (S)?
topic.3.step.longitude.title: Step 2: longitude
topic.3.step.longitude.body: Now find the meridian that goes through the point and read its number at the bottom edge. Is the point right of Greenwich (E) or left of it (W)?
topic.3.step.answer.title: Put it together
topic.3.step.answer.body: The point lies on the 30°N parallel and on the 30°E meridian. Its coordinates are 30°N, 30°E — very close to Cairo.
topic.3.step.between.title: Between the lines
topic.3.step.between.body: If a point lies between two lines, count the degrees. Halfway between 40° and 50° is 45°.
topic.3.step.southwest.title: South and west
topic.3.step.southwest.body: Try this point yourself: which parallel and which meridian go through it? Remember the letters S and W. (Answer: 30°S, 60°W.)
topic.3.step.globe.title: On the globe
topic.3.step.globe.body: The grid works the same way on the globe. Turn the globe to find the point near Sydney: 34°S, 151°E.
topic.3.step.play.title: Try it yourself
topic.3.step.play.body: Drag the point, say its coordinates out loud, then check the answer below the map.
topic.4.step.plan.title: From numbers to a place
topic.4.step.plan.body: Let's find 50°N, 30°E. First find the parallel: 50°N.
topic.4.step.meridian.title: Then the meridian
topic.4.step.meridian.body: Now find the meridian 30°E. Remember: E means to the right of Greenwich.
topic.4.step.cross.title: Where the lines cross
topic.4.step.cross.body: The place is where the two lines cross. It is Kyiv!
topic.4.step.letters.title: Letters matter
topic.4.step.letters.body: 34°S, 151°E is Sydney. But 34°N, 151°W is in the middle of the Pacific Ocean! Always check N or S and E or W.
topic.4.step.play.title: Try it yourself
topic.4.step.play.body: Drag the point to find places, or pick a city from the list and check its coordinates.
topic.5.step.sixty.title: A degree has 60 minutes
topic.5.step.sixty.body: One degree is divided into 60 minutes, written with the sign ′. So 52°30′N is exactly halfway between 52°N and 53°N.
topic.5.step.quarters.title: Halves and quarters
topic.5.step.quarters.body: 30′ is half a degree. 15′ is a quarter of a degree and 45′ is three quarters. This point is at 52°15′N, 21°45′E.
topic.5.step.warsaw.title: Warsaw, exactly
topic.5.step.warsaw.body: The centre of Warsaw is at about 52°14′N, 21°01′E. On a school map we often round it to 52°N, 21°E.
topic.5.step.compare.title: Which is further north?
topic.5.step.compare.body: 52°45′N is north of 52°15′N: the degrees are the same, but it has more minutes. In the Southern Hemisphere more minutes means further south.
topic.5.step.play.title: Try it yourself
topic.5.step.play.body: Each arrow key press moves the point by 1′, and with Shift by 1°. Find 52°30′N, 20°45′E.
topic.6.step.same-lat.title: Same side: subtract
topic.6.step.same-lat.body: Warsaw is at 52°N and Cairo at 30°N. Both are north of the equator, so we subtract: 52 − 30 = 22°.
topic.6.step.opposite-lat.title: Different sides: add
topic.6.step.opposite-lat.body: Cairo is at 30°N and Cape Town at 34°S. The equator lies between them, so we add: 30 + 34 = 64°.
topic.6.step.same-lon.title: Longitude works the same way
topic.6.step.same-lon.body: Kyiv is at 31°E and Warsaw at 21°E. Both are east of Greenwich: 31 − 21 = 10°.
topic.6.step.opposite-lon.title: Across Greenwich: add
topic.6.step.opposite-lon.body: New York is at 74°W and Warsaw at 21°E. Greenwich lies between them: 74 + 21 = 95°.
topic.6.step.over-180.title: More than 180°? Go the other way
topic.6.step.over-180.body: Tokyo is at 140°E and Honolulu at 158°W. 140 + 158 = 298°, which is more than 180°. The shorter way crosses the 180° meridian: 360 − 298 = 62°.
topic.6.step.play.title: Try it yourself
topic.6.step.play.body: Drag the point. How many degrees of latitude and longitude is it from Warsaw (52°N, 21°E)?
topic.7.step.degree-length.title: How long is one degree?
topic.7.step.degree-length.body: A meridian runs from pole to pole: about 20,016 km and 180°. So one degree along a meridian is about 111.2 km.
topic.7.step.example.title: Degrees into kilometres
topic.7.step.example.body: Two points on the same meridian, at 50°N and 40°N, are 10° apart: 10 × 111.2 = 1112 km.
topic.7.step.across-equator.title: Across the equator
topic.7.step.across-equator.body: From 10°N to 20°S along a meridian: 10 + 20 = 30°, so 30 × 111.2 = 3336 km.
topic.7.step.reverse.title: Kilometres into degrees
topic.7.step.reverse.body: If two places on one meridian are 556 km apart, divide: 556 ÷ 111.2 = 5°.
topic.7.step.only-meridians.title: Why only along meridians?
topic.7.step.only-meridians.body: Parallels get shorter towards the poles, so one degree along a parallel is shorter than 111.2 km (except on the equator). That is why we use this rule along meridians.
topic.7.step.play.title: Try it yourself
topic.7.step.play.body: Move the point along the meridian. Its distance from the equator is its latitude × 111.2 km.
topic.8.step.rotation.title: The Earth spins
topic.8.step.rotation.body: The Earth turns once a day, from west to east. The half facing the Sun has day, the other half has night. Drag the time slider and watch night move.
topic.8.step.noon.title: Noon on a meridian
topic.8.step.noon.body: When the Sun is at its highest over a meridian, it is noon — 12:00 local solar time — along that whole meridian, from pole to pole.
topic.8.step.fifteen.title: 15° every hour
topic.8.step.fifteen.body: The Earth turns 360° in 24 hours. That is 15° every hour, and 1° every 4 minutes.
topic.8.step.east-later.title: East is later
topic.8.step.east-later.body: The Sun rises in the east, so places further east have a later solar time. When it is 12:00 in London (0°), it is about 13:24 in Warsaw (21°E): 21 × 4 min = 84 min.
topic.8.step.calculate.title: Let's calculate
topic.8.step.calculate.body: Warsaw (21°E) and Kyiv (31°E) are 10° apart, which is 10 × 4 = 40 minutes. When it is 12:00 solar time in Warsaw, it is 12:40 in Kyiv, because Kyiv is further east.
topic.8.step.seasons.title: Polar day and polar night
topic.8.step.seasons.body: The Earth's axis is tilted. Move the date: around 21 June the area around the North Pole has day all the time, and around 21 December it has night all the time.
topic.8.step.zones.title: Did you know? Time zones
topic.8.step.zones.body: Clocks do not show solar time. A whole country uses one time zone, so in Warsaw the Sun is highest at about 11:36 in winter (10:36 UTC + 1 hour) and about 12:36 in summer (10:36 UTC + 2 hours).
topic.8.step.play.title: Day and night lab
topic.8.step.play.body: Move the time, the date and the point. Watch the clocks and the line of noon.

places.title: Places
q.nameLine.promptPoint: In which two hemispheres is point A?
q.nameLine.explain.equator: The equator is the parallel 0°. It runs around the middle of the Earth.
q.nameLine.explain.prime: The prime meridian is 0°. It goes through Greenwich in London.
q.nameLine.explain.antimeridian: The 180° meridian is on the opposite side of the Earth from Greenwich.
q.nameLine.explain.parallel: This is the parallel {value}. Parallels are circles parallel to the equator.
q.nameLine.explain.meridian: This is the meridian {value}. Meridians join the North Pole and the South Pole.
q.nameLine.explain.tropicCancer: The Tropic of Cancer is the parallel at about 23½°N.
q.nameLine.explain.tropicCapricorn: The Tropic of Capricorn is the parallel at about 23½°S.
q.nameLine.explain.arcticCircle: The Arctic Circle is the parallel at about 66½°N.
q.nameLine.explain.antarcticCircle: The Antarctic Circle is the parallel at about 66½°S.
q.nameLine.explainHemi.N: The Northern Hemisphere is everything north of the equator.
q.nameLine.explainHemi.S: The Southern Hemisphere is everything south of the equator.
q.nameLine.explainHemi.E: The Eastern Hemisphere is everything east of the prime meridian, up to 180°.
q.nameLine.explainHemi.W: The Western Hemisphere is everything west of the prime meridian, up to 180°.
q.nameLine.explainPoint: Point A is at {coords}, so it is in the {nsHemi} and {ewHemi} hemispheres.
q.further.mistake.opposite: That point lies furthest {dir} — the opposite direction!
q.rule.mixed.lat: Any place with N latitude is north of any place with S latitude.
q.rule.mixed.lon: Any place with E longitude is east of any place with W longitude (as long as we do not cross the 180° meridian).
q.rule.bigger.N: In the Northern Hemisphere, a bigger number means further north.
q.rule.bigger.S: In the Southern Hemisphere, a bigger number means further south.
q.rule.bigger.E: In the Eastern Hemisphere, a bigger number means further east.
q.rule.bigger.W: In the Western Hemisphere, a bigger number means further west.
q.rule.zero.lat: Places with N latitude lie north of the equator (0°), places with S latitude lie south of it.
q.rule.zero.lon: Places with E longitude lie east of the prime meridian (0°), places with W longitude lie west of it.
q.relative.prompt.lat: Is point A ({point}) north or south of the parallel {line}?
q.relative.prompt.lon: Is point A ({point}) east or west of the meridian {line}?
q.relative.explain.lat: Point A has latitude {value} and the parallel is {line}, so the point lies {dir} of the parallel. {rule}
q.relative.explain.lon: Point A has longitude {value} and the meridian is {line}, so the point lies {dir} of the meridian. {rule}
q.read.prompt: What are the coordinates of the point?
q.read.explain: The point lies on the parallel {lat} and on the meridian {lon}, so its coordinates are {coords}.
q.place.explain: First find the parallel {lat}, then the meridian {lon}. The point goes where they cross.
q.mistake.nsLetter: Check the letter: N means north of the equator, S means south of it.
q.mistake.ewLetter: Check the letter: E means east of Greenwich, W means west of it.
q.mistake.bothLetters: Both letters are the wrong way round. N or S says up or down, E or W says right or left.
q.mistake.swapped: Latitude and longitude are swapped. Latitude (N or S) always comes first.
q.mistake.minutes: Close! Check the minutes: 30′ is half a degree and 15′ is a quarter of a degree.
q.diff.prompt.lat: What is the difference in latitude between A ({a}) and B ({b})?
q.diff.prompt.lon: What is the difference in longitude between A ({a}) and B ({b})?
q.diff.explain.same.lat: Both points are on the same side of the equator, so subtract: {big} − {small} = {result}°.
q.diff.explain.same.lon: Both points are on the same side of the prime meridian, so subtract: {big} − {small} = {result}°.
q.diff.explain.opposite.lat: The points are on different sides of the equator, so add: {x} + {y} = {result}°.
q.diff.explain.opposite.lon: The points are on different sides of the prime meridian, so add: {x} + {y} = {result}°.
q.diff.explain.zero.lat: One point lies on the equator (0°), so the difference is simply the other number: {result}°.
q.diff.explain.zero.lon: One point lies on the prime meridian (0°), so the difference is simply the other number: {result}°.
q.diff.explain.over180: The points are on different sides of the prime meridian, so add: {x} + {y} = {sum}°. That is more than 180°, so take the shorter way across the 180° meridian: 360 − {sum} = {result}°.
q.diff.mistake.subtracted.lat: You subtracted, but the points are on different sides of the equator. Add the numbers instead.
q.diff.mistake.subtracted.lon: You subtracted, but the points are on different sides of the prime meridian. Add the numbers instead.
q.diff.mistake.added.lat: You added, but both points are on the same side of the equator. Subtract the smaller number from the bigger one.
q.diff.mistake.added.lon: You added, but both points are on the same side of the prime meridian. Subtract the smaller number from the bigger one.
q.diff.mistake.over180: Adding was right, but the sum is more than 180°. Take the shorter way: 360° minus the sum.
q.diff.mistake.subtractedOver180: Don't subtract here: the points are on different sides of the prime meridian. Add the numbers, and because the sum is more than 180°, take 360° minus the sum.
q.dist.prompt: Points A ({a}) and B ({b}) lie on the same meridian. How far apart are they in kilometres?
q.dist.promptReverse: Two places on the same meridian are {km} km apart. How many degrees of latitude apart are they?
q.dist.explain: {diff} One degree along a meridian is about 111.2 km, so {deg} × 111.2 = {km} km.
q.dist.explainReverse: One degree along a meridian is about 111.2 km, so divide: {km} ÷ 111.2 = {deg}°.
q.dist.note111: You used 111 km per degree. That is fine! The more exact value is 111.2 km.
q.dist.mistake.degrees: That is the number of degrees. Multiply it by 111.2 to get kilometres.
q.dist.mistake.multiplied: You multiplied. To turn kilometres into degrees, divide by 111.2.
q.time.prompt.later: Where is the local solar time later: at A ({a}) or at B ({b})?
q.time.explain.later.east: {rule} So B is further east than A. The Sun reaches places further east earlier, so the local solar time at B is later.
q.time.explain.later.west: {rule} So A is further east than B. The Sun reaches places further east earlier, so the local solar time at A is later.
q.time.rule.across180.east: The shorter way from A to B is only {deg}° and it leads east, across the 180° meridian, where E longitude changes into W longitude.
q.time.rule.across180.west: The shorter way from A to B is only {deg}° and it leads west, across the 180° meridian, where W longitude changes into E longitude.
q.time.prompt.clock: At A ({a}) it is {time} local solar time. What is the local solar time at B ({b})?
q.time.minutes: Each 1° is 4 minutes of time: {deg} × 4 = {min} min.
q.time.minutesLong: Each 1° is 4 minutes of time: {deg} × 4 = {min} min = {duration}.
q.time.calc.east: {rule} B is further east, so its time is later: {timeA} + {min} min = {timeB}.
q.time.calc.eastNextDay: {rule} B is further east, so its time is later: {timeA} + {min} min = {timeB} the next day.
q.time.calc.eastPrevDay: {rule} B is further east, so its time is later: {timeA} + {min} min = {timeB}. But going east across the 180° meridian the date goes back one day, so at B it is still the day before.
q.time.calc.west: {rule} B is further west, so its time is earlier: {timeA} − {min} min = {timeB}.
q.time.calc.westPrevDay: {rule} B is further west, so its time is earlier: {timeA} − {min} min = {timeB} the day before.
q.time.calc.westNextDay: {rule} B is further west, so its time is earlier: {timeA} − {min} min = {timeB}. But going west across the 180° meridian the date moves forward one day, so at B it is already the next day.
q.time.prompt.degrees: The local solar time in two places differs by {duration}. How many degrees of longitude apart are the two places?
q.time.explain.degrees: {duration} = {min} min. Every 4 minutes of time make 1° of longitude: {min} ÷ 4 = {deg}°.
q.time.explain.degreesShort: Every 4 minutes of time make 1° of longitude: {min} ÷ 4 = {deg}°.
q.time.mistake.direction: Wrong direction! Further east means a later time, further west means an earlier time.
q.time.mistake.over180: Across the 180° meridian take the shorter way: 360° minus the sum. And remember that further east means a later time.
q.time.mistake.perDegree: Remember: 1° of longitude is 4 minutes of time, not 1 minute.
q.time.mistake.minutes: That is the number of minutes. Divide it by 4 to get degrees.
q.time.mistake.multiplied: Do not multiply here: to turn minutes into degrees, divide by 4.
